title: 💣 Creative destruction prepares to go public
body_text: Dutch company Robin Radar was formed five decades ago to produce unique radar systems designed to detect birds, mostly to ensure that planes landing at major airports can avoid dangerous flocks. This was a solid and reliable business for a while, a charming little niche of detecting speedy, small airborne organisms that can cause large problems for expensive infrastructure and endanger human life. Then, of course, came drones, and then the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and then the shifting reality of warfare towards cheap, flimsy drones loaded up with explosives. Yet again, a new form of the core problem solved by Robin Radar — detecting speedy, small airborne robots that can cause large problems for expensive infrastructure and endanger human life — emerged, and needless to say business has really taken off . Bloomberg reports that Anthropic, which had been known to be eyeing an IPO sometime after November’s mid-term elections, is aiming to go public before Thanksgiving . Earlier this week, Reuters scored a copy of the Anthropic prospectus , and traders have spent the last several days digesting it. To say that the numbers in the report are jaw-dropping and eye-popping is an insult to mandibular and ocular versatility. On one hand, the good numbers: Revenue 12x’d in 2025, hitting $4.6 billion, though they lost $8 billion on an operating basis. They spent $7.33 billion on compute alone, which was more than half of the $12.65 billion in operating expenses. Big numbers, but not exactly shocking. On the other, the bad ones: “On an operating basis” excludes writedowns of liabilities related to previous fundraising; the company reported a net loss of $42 billion in 2025. Still, those numbers are still downright small, compared to… The crazy one? Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on cloud. A half-trillion on cloud. That’s the kind of number that gets people thinking this better be worth it. Then, of course, the only one that really matters: how much this company's gonna be worth. For that, SpaceX is the bar to beat, and reportedly Anthropic is eyeing $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion. Earlier this year, SpaceX's IPO managed to underscore just how little revenue investors really needed to see to grant a multi-trillion dollar valuation. One reason for the interest at any price? So far, the only way that investors in public markets have managed to invest in AI laboratories has been indirectly. Either they've bought the companies that supply these labs — the chip manufacturers, the data center operators — as an implicit bet on the ultimate demand for this tech. The other alternative is investing in the hyperscalers — Alphabet and Meta — who have an AI lab as a subsidiary, the downside being that the actual AI laboratory's impact on their share prices is a mere drop in the bucket compared to the vast amounts of valuation derived from their mature advertising business. The last way to get in on the trade as an investor in public markets would, presumably, be to bet against the long-term performance of the companies that will be disrupted by the tech. When one public company does something that takes market share from another public company, investors are able to react by buying the former and selling the latter, in the aggregate increasing the valuation of the former and reducing the valuation of the latter. But when a non-public AI lab revealed that they were able to compete with the core offerings of a public company, things are less direct: recall the hits taken by the trucking business, the cybersecurity business , the SaaS business , and the consulting business whenever a white paper implied that OpenAI or Anthropic was poised to eat their lunch. This led to the interesting paradox where, essentially, private Anthropic would release tech demonstration that would destroy a lot of the value of a cohort of public companies, but there was no direct commensurate creation of value elsewhere in the stock market. title: 🙅‍♂️ Refusin’ Texas
body_text: After launching its $499 AI-powered CameraJet toothbrush earlier this month, things haven’t been running smoothly for Dyson: the company was forced to withdraw the impressive (and impressively expensive) model from certain markets , as customers across the world took to social media to complain about various faults. Execs were initially tight-lipped about what exactly was going wrong with the CameraJet — which was trained on 470,000 dental images, has a 100,000-pixel macro lens, and jets short bursts of water into affected areas of the mouth like a water flosser — but have now told Bloomberg , presumably through gritted teeth, that “water seepage” was behind the malfunctioning early batch of brushes. There are songs that become so ubiquitous in modern life that they pass unchallenged into the modern music canon and wider public consciousness; trotted out for mass singalongs when the occasion demands: “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” before we’ve even taken Halloween decorations down; “Seven Nation Army,” at literally any sporting event anywhere in the world; “Wonderwall,” when the party has taken one too many wrong turns and the inevitable guitar is wielded. Although it’s now 24 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” most people agree, is not one of those songs. The song’s undeniable hook and the country-pop songstress’s sultry vocals aside, vast swaths of the music-listening public are queuing up to announce, sometimes proudly , that they’ve never heard the longest-reigning number one of all time. That might have something to do with how a lot of us have started finding new music. Billboard staff writer Kyle Denis says he isn’t surprised by the idea that there’s a song at the top of the charts for six months that a lot of people have never knowingly heard, as mainstream culture splinters into “incredibly optimized and hyper-individualized algorithmic silos and digital echo chambers.” That theory bears out in the responses to a YouGov survey conducted and published earlier this month. According to the poll, 59% of US adults who listen to music more than they did last year discover new music through streaming service recommendations, while 52% are finding songs via social media and music blogs. That marks a clear shift toward personal methods of picking up new music of late, as more traditional methods of song discovery like listening to the radio, music TV channels, and recommendations from family and friends slip down the list. As the monoculture recedes further into the rearview mirror with algorithms and for-you pages corroding the shared cultural experience that radio stations and mainstream television once helped to cultivate, it’s little wonder that we live in a world where a lot of Americans couldn’t begin to hum the melody of (on paper) one of the biggest songs in modern music. Whether or not you had an active choice in “Choosin’ Texas” becoming the song of 2026, you should probably get comfortable with the idea of megahits you’ve never heard before. title: 🏛️ Wall Street has big expectations for Micron
body_text: Lidl has finally solved the age-old problem of grocery shopping sober. After failing to get a license to sell alcohol at a new Northern Ireland store, the German supermarket found a workaround: open a pub inside the store, the Wall Street Journal reports . The Middle Ale (named after Lidl’s famously bargain-packed middle aisle) has proven so popular that the supermarket now employs bouncers to keep the crowds in check. Police were even called to break up a fight on opening night. Stocks were mixed on Tuesday as long-term Treasury yields rose to their highest level since 2002. Expectations are high as Micron Technology , the American chipmaker that’s become central to the artificial intelligence memory boom, prepares to report Q4 earnings results on today after the bell. Micron and its semiconductor peers have benefited from surging demand from AI hyperscalers such as Microsoft , Amazon , and Meta combined with industry-wide supply shortages. This tight market environment has given chipmakers strong pricing power, driving sharp sequential price increases. “We see the setup as constructive with multiple beat-and-raise levers still in play against a memory backdrop that remains structurally tight across both DRAM and NAND,” JP Morgan analysts wrote in a Monday note. Per analysts polled by FactSet, Micron is expected to report: $51.3 billion in revenue, including $39.8 billion from DRAM and $12.2 billion from NAND, the two kinds of memory chips Micron sells. That’s above the company’s guidance for revenue, which is between $49 billion to $51 billion. Adjusted earnings per share of $31.72. The company’s guidance for that metric as of its last report is between $30 and $32. To put the AI memory boom into perspective: Micron reported $11.3 billion in revenue and $3.03 in adjusted earnings per share in the same quarter last year. Beyond the quarterly numbers, JPMorgan noted, investors will also be looking for updates on Micron’s push to lock more customers into longer-term supply deals, as well as whether the company could soon put more cash toward buying back its own stock. With 95% of analysts having a “buy” rating on the stock, it's not exactly a hot take to predict that the earnings results will be bullish for the stock. The bigger question is whether Micron can convince investors that the conditions fueling its boom have staying power. “The debate has very clearly shifted from ‘how good can it get?’ to ‘how long can it stay this good,’” Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a Monday note. “That's a debate that can take longer to win, but we do have conviction in durability.” That’s how much The Monopoly Americana Edition costs.
